Electrophilic addition. An organic reaction where a pi bond in an unsaturated compound, such as an alkene or alkyne, is broken to react with an electron-deficient species—an electrophile—resulting in the formation of two new sigma bonds. This reaction class is the primary method for functionalizing carbon-carbon double and triple bonds.

In hydrohalogenation reactions, the reaction obeys Markovnikov's rule, which dictates that the hydrogen atom adds to the carbon with the greater number of hydrogens. This regioselectivity is dictated by the formation of the more stable carbocation intermediate. During halogenation—the addition of chlorine or bromine—the reaction proceeds via a cyclic halonium ion, which blocks one face of the molecule to force an anti-addition stereochemical outcome.

A key exception is hydroboration-oxidation, a two-step reaction that bypasses Markovnikov regioselectivity to yield the anti-Markovnikov alcohol via a concerted syn-addition of boron and hydrogen. Reactions like acid-catalyzed hydration are subject to carbocation rearrangements, such as hydride or alkyl shifts, which occur to form a more stable carbocation. To avoid these rearrangements, chemists use oxymercuration-demercuration, which utilizes a cyclic mercurinium ion intermediate to cleanly yield the Markovnikov hydration product.

The reaction enables the production of organic halides through the addition of hydrogen halides like hydrochloric acid, hydrobromic acid, or hydroiodic acid to alkenes. Similarly, both acid-catalyzed hydration and hydroboration-oxidation of alkenes yield alcohols, while mercury(II) acetate is the electrophilic reagent used to form the cyclic intermediate in oxymercuration reactions.
